writers.name: Dawn Sherill-Porter
writers.dek: Content editor at Lifeway Christian Resources | Writes for Lifeway Research on Bible reading habits and discipleship
writers.bio: Dawn Sherill-Porter is a content editor for Lifeway Christian Resources and writes for Lifeway Research on personal Bible reading, including why reading plans stall and how busy Christians and pastors keep a daily habit.

start_here.title: How to Stay in the Word, Even When You're Busy
start_here.note: Argues that a daily Bible habit survives a full calendar when it is treated as the foundation of the day rather than one more task, and applies that to pastors' own reading.

start_here.title: Why Bible Reading Plans Fail (and What We Can Do About It)
start_here.note: Looks at why church members start a reading plan with enthusiasm and drift into obligation or apathy, and asks what leaders can do to help a plan last.

topics.angle: Why daily Bible reading stalls and how to keep it going.
Building a Bible reading habit into a full calendar.
Helping church members finish a reading plan.

writers.review_notes: Lifeway Research lists only two pieces by her, so Start here has two picks, not three. No other outlet found.

writers.name: Alex Harris
writers.dek: Attorney and Keller Center fellow | Coauthor of Do Hard Things | Writes for The Gospel Coalition on faith, mortality, and public life
writers.bio: Alex Harris is an attorney and a fellow at The Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics. As a teenager he coauthored Do Hard Things: A Teenage Rebellion Against Low Expectations with his twin brother, Brett. A graduate of Harvard Law School, he worked as a law clerk for U.S. Supreme Court Justices Neil Gorsuch and Anthony Kennedy.

where_they_write.outlet: The Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics

start_here.title: Redeem the Time: What Ben Sasse Teaches Us About Life, Death, and Politics
start_here.note: Draws on Ben Sasse's public reflections after a terminal cancer diagnosis to set out a framework for what matters most in life, death, and politics.

start_here.title: Alex Harris: How to Do Hard Things
start_here.note: Interview with Sarah Eekhoff Zylstra about clerking for two U.S. Supreme Court justices and about his brother Joshua Harris's public deconstruction of his faith.

start_here.title: Gospel Hope for Gen Z Ministry
start_here.note: Panel with Rachel Gilson, Kori Porter, and Derek Rishmawy on signs of renewal among Gen Z; Harris speaks on faithful presence.

topics.angle: What Ben Sasse's terminal diagnosis teaches about facing death.
Lessons for political life from a former senator's last chapter.
Ministry to Gen Z and the practice of faithful presence.

writers.review_notes: Identity confirmed: the Alex Harris on our site is the byline on the TGC Ben Sasse piece (homepage and digest, 2026-04-29), and TGC's profile for that byline is the attorney and Do Hard Things coauthor. writers.name: Brandon Corley
writers.dek: MDiv student at Southern Seminary | Writes for American Reformer on Baptist political theology and natural law
writers.bio: Brandon Corley is a graduate of The Master's University, where he earned a degree in Biblical Studies, and an MDiv student at The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary. He writes for American Reformer on Baptist political theology and natural law.

start_here.title: In Defense of the Baptist State
start_here.note: Argues that Baptists have no principled reason to reject an established Baptist religion, drawing on a 1659 declaration by Baptistic Congregationalists in London.

start_here.title: On Baptist Establishment, Again
start_here.note: A follow-up that sets out the political principles behind the earlier essay and sketches what a Christian establishment could look like in America today.

start_here.title: The Natural End of Man
start_here.note: Argues from the classical idea of natural ends that human nature is ordered to knowing and loving God, and considers natural virtue in that light.

topics.angle: The case for a Baptist establishment.
Establishment arguments within the Reformed political tradition.
Toleration and its limits in early Baptist confessions.
Seventeenth-century Baptist declarations on toleration.

writers.name: Chandler Vannoy
writers.dek: Lifeway Leadership | Co-host of 5 Leadership Questions | Writes for RELEVANT on Bible reading and discerning God's will
writers.bio: Chandler Vannoy is a graduate of the University of Tennessee and holds a Master of Divinity from The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary. His RELEVANT author bio lists him as brand manager for Lifeway Leadership at Lifeway Christian Resources, and he has co-hosted Lifeway Leadership's 5 Leadership Questions podcast. He has written for RELEVANT since 2019 on Bible reading and decision making.

start_here.title: What We Get Wrong About 'Finding God's Will'
start_here.note: Argues that anxiety about finding God's will comes from treating it as a hidden path to uncover, and points readers to a God bigger than any single decision.

start_here.title: How to Move Beyond Instagrammable Bible Reading
start_here.note: Argues that a diet of short, shareable verses trains short attention spans, and calls for slower, sustained reading of Scripture.

start_here.title: Habits, Bible Reading and New Year's Resolutions
start_here.note: Argues that resolutions to read the Bible more usually fail for lack of a place on the calendar, and that a scheduled habit does better than good intentions.

topics.angle: Moving past verse snippets to sustained reading.
Putting Bible reading on the calendar.
Anxiety about finding God's will.

writers.name: David Powlison
writers.dek: Biblical counselor, 1949-2019 | Executive director of CCEF, 2014-2019 | Wrote on idolatry, suffering, and pastoral counsel
writers.bio: David Powlison (1949-2019) served as executive director of the Christian Counseling & Educational Foundation (CCEF) from 2014 to 2019, as a faculty member, and as senior editor of the Journal of Biblical Counseling. He held a PhD from the University of Pennsylvania and an MDiv from Westminster Theological Seminary. He wrote extensively on biblical counseling and on the relationship between faith and psychology, including the books Seeing with New Eyes and Speaking Truth in Love.

bio_sources.label: In Loving Memory of David Powlison, CCEF

where_they_write.outlet: CCEF and the Journal of Biblical Counseling

start_here.title: Idols of the Heart and "Vanity Fair"
start_here.note: Argues that idolatry is the category that explains both a person's inner motivations and the pull of cultural values, worked through two counseling case studies.

start_here.title: An Open Letter to the Suffering Christian
start_here.note: A pastoral letter that begins with listening and points a hurting believer to Jesus as a sympathetic friend, fellow sufferer, and Savior.

start_here.title: Why Pastors Have a Unique Responsibility to Counsel
start_here.note: Argues that counseling is part of every pastor's calling rather than an optional specialty, and sets out how pastoral counsel differs from the counseling professions.

start_here.title: An Open Letter to Those Debilitated by Their Sexual Sin
start_here.note: Written to Christians weighed down by repeated failure, guilt, and shame, starting from a friend's slow change after conversion.

start_here.title: The Right Kind of Weakness
start_here.note: Remarks prepared for Westminster Theological Seminary graduates shortly before his death, reading the Sermon on the Mount as a call to the weakness that receives God's strength.

topics.angle: Biblical counseling and the relationship of faith and psychology.
Pastoral letters to Christians who are suffering.
Why counseling belongs to every pastor.
Help for Christians caught in repeated sexual sin.

writers.name: Jeremy Kimble
writers.dek: Professor of systematic and applied theology at Cedarville University | Author of Behold and Become | Writes for The Gospel Coalition and Christ Over All on Scripture, doctrine, and the church
writers.bio: Jeremy Kimble is professor of systematic and applied theology at Cedarville University and holds a PhD from Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary. He is the author of Behold and Become: Reading Scripture for Transformation, How Can I Get More Out of My Bible Reading?, and 40 Questions About Church Membership and Discipline, and coauthor with Ched Spellman of Invitation to Biblical Theology. He served in pastoral ministry for eight years and is a member and minister at University Baptist Church.

start_here.title: Lies and a Lion: Making Sense of 1 Kings 13
start_here.note: Reads the strange story of the man of God and the old prophet within the structure of 1 and 2 Kings and argues it calls God's people to receive and fully obey his word rather than follow religious leaders astray.

start_here.title: The Sovereignty of God
start_here.note: Sets out God's sovereignty as final authority over creation, human decisions, and salvation, links it to providence and concurrence, and argues against process and open theism.

start_here.title: How Should One Understand One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic?
start_here.note: Explains the four marks of the church in the Nicene Creed and argues that Protestants can affirm each one without accepting Roman Catholic claims.

topics.angle: Reading Scripture for transformation and getting more from Bible reading.
The biblical and historical case for church discipline, from 1 Corinthians 5 to Jonathan Edwards.
What church membership is and why it matters.
God's sovereignty over human decisions and salvation.

writers.review_notes: Old page called him an author and apologist; he is a Cedarville theology professor. TGC dates the curated piece Apr 15, 2026 (we curated it Apr 19). Themelios pieces left out because their pages show no date.

writers.name: Christopher Gehrz
writers.dek: Professor of history at Bethel University | Author of a religious biography of Charles Lindbergh | Writes for Mere Orthodoxy and The Pietist Schoolman on Christianity, history, and education
writers.bio: Christopher Gehrz is professor of history at Bethel University in St. Paul, Minnesota, where he has taught since 2003, and holds a PhD in history from Yale University. He is the author of Charles Lindbergh: A Religious Biography of America's Most Infamous Pilot (2021) and coauthor of The Pietist Option: Hope for the Renewal of Christianity (2017). He writes about Christianity, history, and education in his Substack newsletter, The Pietist Schoolman.

start_here.title: Christians in the Age of Hitler
start_here.note: Reviews Alec Ryrie's The Age of Hitler and How We Will Survive It, which holds that the Western moral consensus built on opposing Nazism is weakening, and asks what role Christians might play in what follows.

start_here.title: The Moral Vision of American Leaders
start_here.note: Reviews Marvin Olasky's Moral Vision, which uses short biographies of presidents to argue that character should guide voters, and questions both its omissions and its likely effect on committed voters.

start_here.title: The Challenge of Graven Images
start_here.note: Looks at the Charles Lindbergh statue at the Minnesota State Capitol and argues that historians should portray his full record, including his eugenics and antisemitism, while honoring the image of God in the people he dismissed.

topics.angle: Pietism and its place in the history of evangelicalism.
A historian's reading of evangelical identity and renewal.
The purpose and future of Christian higher education.
Character, democracy, and the moral consensus of the postwar West.

writers.review_notes: The duplicate page chris-gehrz was merged into this one on 2026-11-12 (merge_duplicate_voices.py: noindex redirect stub, removed from sitemap and index). Old bio wrongly called him author of The Pietist Vision of Christian Higher Education (Bethel lists him as editor). Substack posts are mostly paywalled, so picks come from Mere Orthodoxy and Current.

writers.name: Glenn A. Moots
writers.dek: Professor of political science and philosophy at Northwood University | Author of Politics Reformed | Writes for American Reformer on Protestant political thought and the American founding
writers.bio: Glenn A. Moots is Professor and Department Chair of Political Science and Philosophy at Northwood University, where he has taught since 1993. He is the author of Politics Reformed: The Anglo-American Legacy of Covenant Theology (2010) and coeditor, with Phillip Hamilton, of Justifying Revolution: Law, Virtue, and Violence in the American War of Independence (2018). He holds a PhD from Louisiana State University and a BA from the University of Michigan. He writes for American Reformer and Law & Liberty on Protestant political thought, religious liberty, and the American founding.

start_here.title: How Radical Was the American Revolution?
start_here.note: Adapted from a Hillsdale College lecture, it questions Bernard Bailyn's radical reading of the Revolution and argues that the convictions of colonial Christians, including Jonathan Mayhew's 1750 sermon on resisting tyrants, were an essential cause of independence.

start_here.title: Protestant Constitutionalism and American Independence
start_here.note: Argues that the Declaration of Independence drew on an older Protestant tradition of resistance, including readings of Romans 13 and the duty of lesser magistrates to restrain a tyrant, rather than on new principles original to Jefferson.

start_here.title: Why Does America Have Religious Liberty?
start_here.note: Reviews Vincent Phillip Muñoz's Religious Liberty and the American Founding and argues that its natural rights reading credits Jefferson too heavily and leaves out the wider Protestant thinking on church and civil magistrate.

start_here.title: Was the Protestant Reformation a Radical Revolution?
start_here.note: Responds to critics such as Patrick Deneen and Brad Gregory by arguing that the Magisterial Reformation preserved social order and classical virtue rather than seeding individualism and liberalism.

topics.angle: Protestant resistance theory and the case for American independence.
How religious liberty emerged at the American founding.
Whether the Reformation was a radical break with Christian social order.
Covenant theology's legacy in Anglo-American politics.

writers.review_notes: Old page said Grove City College; every source says Northwood University. Three book titles in the old data were not found anywhere and were dropped. Publisher dates (May 19, Jul 9) differ from our curated dates (May 28, Jul 20).

writers.name: James Abernathy
writers.dek: Attorney in First Amendment litigation | Writes for The Gospel Coalition and on Substack on disability, the body, and the dignity of dependence
writers.bio: James Abernathy is an attorney who specializes in litigation defending First Amendment rights. He holds an MA from Fuller Theological Seminary and a JD from Regent University School of Law. A quadriplegic since a spinal cord injury in high school, he writes and speaks to advocate for the body and the dignity of dependence.

start_here.title: Why I'm a Disabled Person, Not a Person with a Disability
start_here.note: Argues that the body is part of a person's identity as God's image bearer, and so rejects the person-first language that separates dignity from disability.

start_here.title: Broken Bodies Make Beautiful Temples
start_here.note: Argues from the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit that bodies marked by disability or illness belong to God and should be trusted to his purposes, not remade by the self.

start_here.title: My Disabled Body is My Forever Body (Being God's Image, Part V)
start_here.note: Argues that God will raise and glorify the same bodies believers have now, so the present body, including its disability, should be honored rather than despised.

start_here.title: Will There Be Disability at the Resurrection? Part 1: Six Guiding Principles
start_here.note: Sets out six scriptural principles for asking whether disability remains after the resurrection, beginning with competing definitions of disability.

topics.angle: Disability, dependence, and God's purposes in the body.
The body as part of what it means to bear God's image.
Whether disability remains in the resurrection body.

writers.review_notes: The quadriplegia line comes from his own Substack About page. Family details (husband, father of two) are on the TGC profile but left out. Employer not named in any source.

writers.name: Derek Rishmawy
writers.dek: RUF campus minister at UC Irvine | Cohost of the Mere Fidelity podcast | Writes for The Gospel Coalition and Mere Orthodoxy on Christian hope, doctrine, and ministry to young adults
writers.bio: Derek Rishmawy (PhD, Trinity Evangelical Divinity School) is the Reformed University Fellowship (RUF) campus minister at the University of California, Irvine. He contributes to Mere Orthodoxy, Christianity Today, and The Gospel Coalition, and writes at his own blog, Reformedish. He cohosts the Mere Fidelity podcast and hosts the What Christians Believe podcast at byFaith.

start_here.title: Where Doomers Can Find Hope
start_here.note: Argues that Christian hope begins with honesty about how often history has brought disaster and rests on God's restraint, renewal in Christ, and allegiance to his kingdom over earthly institutions.

start_here.title: Ministry After the Boomer Apocalypse
start_here.note: Remarks to the PCA Next Generation Forum arguing that the coming generational turnover and wider dechurching call for exegetical, catechetical, and apologetic preaching, hospitality, and deliberate pastor training.

start_here.title: In Praise of My Youth Pastor
start_here.note: A memorial essay on the youth pastor who let him preach as a teenager and later mentored him, presented as a model of investing in young people.

start_here.title: Gospel Hope for Gen-Z Ministry
start_here.note: Panel with Rachel Gilson, Alex Harris, and Kori Porter on openness to the gospel among Gen Z and the challenges of discipling new believers into the local church.

topics.angle: Christian hope against cultural doomerism.
Campus ministry and reaching Gen Z.
Preaching and pastor training as the church changes generations.

writers.name: J. A. Medders
writers.dek: Director of theology and content, Send Network | Author of Humble Calvinism and Gospel Formed | Writes at Spiritual Theology on Spurgeon, the Puritans, and the Christian life
writers.bio: J. A. Medders is the director of theology and content for Send Network and the general editor for New Churches. He is also a fellow of The Spurgeon Library and visiting professor of Christian studies at Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary. He earned a PhD in biblical spirituality at The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary under Donald S. Whitney. He is the author of Gospel Formed and Humble Calvinism, coauthor of The Soul-Winning Church, and writes the Spiritual Theology newsletter.

bio_sources.label: Author page, The Good Book Company

start_here.title: It is Finished!
start_here.note: A Good Friday meditation on John 19:30 arguing that every Old Testament sacrifice, symbol, and promise is fulfilled in Christ's dying cry.

start_here.title: How the Puritans Helped J. I. Packer
start_here.note: Draws on J. I. Packer's account of seven ways the Puritans shaped him and recommends seven Puritan books as starting points.

start_here.title: His Name Stands Above Them All
start_here.note: Walks through the biblical names of God and sets them against the rulers and ideas they outlast, ending with Psalm 148:13.

Spurgeon and the Puritans as guides for the Christian life.
Biblical spirituality drawn from older Reformed writers.
Theological training for church planters through Send Network.

writers.name: Joshua Budimlic
writers.dek: Teacher and writer | Blogs at Iotas in Eternity | Writes for The Gospel Coalition Canada and SOLA Network on conversion, grief, and the hope of heaven
writers.bio: Joshua Budimlic is a teacher and writer who, in his own words, hopes to bring together his passion for theology, education, and literature in serving the next generation. He blogs at Iotas in Eternity, where he often writes about C.S. Lewis, heaven, and the life and death of his father, and his essays have also appeared at The Gospel Coalition Canada and SOLA Network.

start_here.title: The Watchmaker's Wager
start_here.note: Sets Pascal's Wager beside his late father's habit, as a watchmaker, of asking elderly customers whether they had been born again, and tells how one of those conversations came back to him years later.

start_here.title: Great Expectations
start_here.note: Reads the healed man of Mark 5, whom Jesus sent home rather than letting him follow, as a word to Christians whose lives stay in one ordinary place.

start_here.title: How Pleasantly the Lines Have Fallen
start_here.note: Works from Psalm 16 to argue that God himself, not a person's circumstances, is the believer's portion, so every Christian's lot has fallen in pleasant places.

start_here.title: Thoroughly Converted: Enslaving the Inner Man for the Glory of Christ
start_here.note: Starts from Walter Hooper's description of C.S. Lewis as the most thoroughly converted man he knew and argues that this is a matter of sanctification, not of being more or less justified.

start_here.title: The Land of Many Meetings
start_here.note: Recalls his father falling ill on Thanksgiving Day and looks ahead to the reunion of believers with Christ and with those who have died before them.

topics.angle: What it means to be thoroughly converted, after C.S. Lewis.
Writing through his father's illness and death.
Heaven as the reunion that earthly longing points to.
Everyday witness in his father's work as a watchmaker.

writers.name: Dallas Willard
writers.dek: Philosopher at USC, 1965 to 2012 | Author of The Divine Conspiracy | Wrote on discipleship, spiritual formation and the kingdom of God
writers.bio: Dallas Willard (1935 to 2013) was born in Buffalo, Missouri, and taught philosophy at the University of Southern California from 1965 until his retirement at the end of 2012, directing its School of Philosophy from 1982 to 1985. He finished his BA at Baylor University, did his PhD work at the University of Wisconsin, and was ordained as a Baptist minister. His books include The Divine Conspiracy, The Spirit of the Disciplines, Renovation of the Heart and Hearing God, along with translations of and a book on the philosopher Edmund Husserl. He taught in Fuller's DMin program and worked with Gary W. Moon to develop the Renovaré Institute for Spiritual Formation.

start_here.title: Spiritual Formation: What it is, and How it is Done
start_here.note: Defines spiritual formation as the transformation of the heart or will so that Christlike action flows from the whole person, and sets out its progression as vision, intention and method.

start_here.title: The Need, Vision and Strategy of Growing in Christlikeness
start_here.note: Argues that everyone is being formed in some direction and proposes a repeatable path for dropping patterns such as anger, contempt and lust through understanding, intention and practical disciplines.

start_here.title: Rethinking Evangelism
start_here.outlet: Dallas Willard Ministries (first published in Cutting Edge, Vineyard USA)
start_here.note: Argues that evangelism which reduces salvation to forgiveness of guilt leaves life unchanged, and calls for evangelism that grows out of a community of disciples living under God's reign.

start_here.title: Jesus as Logician and Apologist
start_here.note: Argues that apologetics should be a helping ministry modeled on Jesus, listening to real questions and using simple logic to aid understanding rather than to win arguments.

topics.angle: Discipleship to Jesus as the heart of the Christian life and of evangelism.
The disciplines as practical means of character change.
Spiritual formation as the transformation of the will toward Christlikeness.
Apologetics as a helping ministry modeled on Jesus.
Evangelism that invites people into life under God's reign, not only forgiveness.

writers.name: Roger Olson
writers.dek: Professor of Christian theology at Truett Seminary, Baylor, 1999 to 2021 | Author of The Story of Christian Theology | Writes on Arminian theology, evangelicalism and historical theology
writers.bio: Roger E. Olson taught Christian theology for 40 years at three Christian universities and retired in 2021 from Baylor University's George W. Truett Theological Seminary, where he was professor of Christian theology from 1999 and Foy Valentine Professor of Christian Theology and Ethics. Before Truett he taught for 15 years at Bethel University in Minnesota. He is a graduate of North American Baptist Seminary and earned a PhD at Rice University in 1984, with research under Wolfhart Pannenberg at the University of Munich. He is the author of more than twenty books, including The Story of Christian Theology and The Journey of Modern Theology, and writes the blog Roger E. Olson at Patheos.

bio_sources.label: Good and Faithful Servants (retired faculty), Truett Seminary, Baylor University, 2024
Endowed professorship announcement, Baylor University news, 2013

start_here.title: Don't Hate Me Because I'm Arminian
start_here.note: Argues that Reformed theologians who deny that Arminians are authentically evangelical are fracturing the evangelical coalition, and calls both camps to mutual respect.

start_here.title: Calvinism and Arminianism Compared
start_here.outlet: Society of Evangelical Arminians (from his Patheos blog)
start_here.note: A teaching handout for Sunday school and small groups that defines classical Calvinism and Arminianism side by side and argues that the real dividing line is not free will but the character of God.

start_here.title: Arminianism is God-Centered Theology
start_here.note: Argues that classical Arminianism affirms human depravity and total dependence on grace, and that it rejects Calvinist determinism chiefly because it would make God the author of sin.

start_here.title: Arminianism FAQ 1 (Everything You Always Wanted to Know…)
start_here.outlet: Society of Evangelical Arminians (from his Patheos blog)
start_here.note: Explains classical Arminianism in question and answer form, covering prevenient grace, resistible grace, conditional election and where it sits between Calvinism and semi-Pelagianism.

topics.angle: The case for classical Arminianism against Calvinist determinism.
Whether Arminians belong in the evangelical coalition, and evangelical identity more broadly.
The story of Christian theology from the early church to modern theology.
Liberal and progressive theology, written from outside conservative evangelicalism.

writers.name: Tony Reinke
writers.dek: Senior teacher at Desiring God and host of Ask Pastor John | Author of 12 Ways Your Phone Is Changing You | Writes on technology, joy and the Christian life
writers.bio: Tony Reinke is senior teacher and lead curator for Desiring God, which he joined in 2012, and the creator, producer and host of the Ask Pastor John podcast with John Piper. Before that he was editorial and research assistant to C.J. Mahaney at Sovereign Grace Ministries from 2008 to 2011. He has written seven books: Lit! A Christian Guide to Reading Books (2011), Newton on the Christian Life (2015), 12 Ways Your Phone Is Changing You (2017), The Joy Project (2018), Competing Spectacles (2019), God, Technology, and the Christian Life (2022) and Ask Pastor John (2024).
